dossier.public_summary: The 0.64-day dip lines up exactly with the star’s rapid rotation and shows a huge brightness swing between dips, larger than the dip itself and on the star itself per centroid. Its long duration is also inconsistent with a small planet around this cool M dwarf. Together this points to stellar variability from a tidally synchronized close companion / active star rather than a planet transit.

reasons.why: Signal is not a transit shape alone: there is a ~1.9% swing at the 0.639 d period, larger than the 1.68% dip and with very high chi2, exactly as expected for a close stellar companion or strong ellipsoidal/synchronous variation, not a planet occultation.

The measured variability period is identical to the dip period in every sector, with spot amplitudes of 30-50k ppm (much larger than the dip). The transit is effectively locked to stellar rotation, so the dip is better explained by the star’s own modulated signal, not an independent planet orbit.

Duration is 1.69x central for this M dwarf and the light-curve density penalty is extreme, indicating the flat-bottomed shape does not correspond to a planet transiting this star but to stellar variation folded at the rotation period.

Difference imaging puts the variation on the target and rules out the few neighbours that could cause the depth, so this is not a background eclipsing binary/blend; the explanation is on the star itself.
